label: Statistics
overview: SAT statistics questions cover mean, median, mode, range, and standard deviation; interpreting data displays (box plots, histograms, dot plots); and understanding what changes to a data set do to these measures. You also need to understand margin of error, sample vs. population, and when a statistical claim is valid.

keyFormulas.name: Median
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Middle value when data is ordered (or avg of two middle values)}

keyFormulas.name: Standard deviation (concept)
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Larger SD} \implies \text{data more spread out from mean}

workedExamples.problem: A data set has values 4, 7, 7, 9, 13. A new value of 40 is added. What happens to the mean and median?

steps.title: Find new mean and median after adding 40
steps.content: New list (ordered): 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 40. Mean = 80/6 ≈ 13.3. Median = average of 7 and 9 = 8.

steps.title: Compare
steps.content: Mean increased significantly (8 → 13.3). Median increased only slightly (7 → 8). The outlier 40 has a much larger effect on the mean.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to sort the data before finding the median
commonMistakes.fix: Always order values from least to greatest first, then identify the middle value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking standard deviation measures the average value rather than spread
commonMistakes.fix: Standard deviation measures how far values are from the mean on average. A high SD means data is spread out; a low SD means data is clustered near the mean.

quickTip: On SAT stat questions, ask yourself: is the question about the centre (mean/median) or spread (range/SD)? Then ask: are there outliers that would pull the mean away from the median? Those two questions cover most stat scenarios.
